The image was captured by a remote camera set up by filmmaker Paolo. — Photo courtesy of Paolo Volponi IPOH: What started as a study of tiny moths led a Polish entomologist and her filmmaker husband deep into the Royal Belum rainforest, where their focus shifted to the critically endangered Malayan tiger. Marta Skowron Volponi, 36, began her scientific expedition in Taman Negara back in 2012, where she discovered the scarlata nirvana, a striking red clearwing moth species. She first visited Royal Belum in 2018 after being introduced to the area by a Malaysian friend. She later teamed up with her husband, Paolo Volponi, combining research and filmmaking to support conservation and education efforts. Her visit only lasted two days, but she was captivated by Royal Belum’s lakes, hilltop forests and largely unexplored surroundings. “My research took an unexpected turn when I found Malayan tiger footprints in the same habitat where I discovered the moths,” she said in an interview. Marta said she and Paolo began documenting the lives of those on the conservation frontlines, threats facing the tiger and the fragile ecosystem. Using remote cameras and accompanying anti-poaching teams into the forest, the couple captured rare glimpses of Malayan tigers and other elusive wildlife while documenting conservation efforts in Royal Belum, one of the world’s oldest rain­forests. Their pursuit faced several setbacks – the Covid-19 pandemic, Paolo falling ill and Marta suffering a jungle accident – before filming resumed last year. Marta said they worked with park rangers, including Orang Asli ranger Mazlan Enjok, who has spent more than a decade protecting Royal Belum. “Witnessing the removal of snares and hearing accounts of tiger poaching in 2018 made me realise the seriousness of threats facing wildlife in Royal Belum. “Anti-poaching efforts were strengthened that year, with authorities increasing ranger numbers and working with NGOs. “Rangers patrolled the forest for signs of poaching and removed snares,” she said. Paolo, 58, documented the rangers’ efforts, which Marta said often went unnoticed despite their importance. This ultimately shifted their focus to the wider rainforest conservation crisis, centred on the Malayan tiger, which is native to the peninsula. Marta said their documentary, titled The Tiger Spirit, was aimed at audiences from all backgrounds, including those not normally interested in wildlife. She said the focus should extend beyond the Malayan tiger to the wider rainforest ecosystem, with deforestation remaining deeply troubling. “Sometimes I feel like crying when I see huge trees coming out of the forest on trucks,” she said. Paolo said their conservation focus shifted in 2022 after African swine fever severely reduced wild boar, a key prey species for Malayan tigers. The decline disrupted the food chain, forcing predators to venture out of the rainforest and increasing road kills and human-wildlife conflict, including attacks on livestock. “The documentary aims to show not only the threats facing the Malayan tiger, but also the beauty of the animal and its forest habitat. “Our remote cameras have captured the tigers displaying individual behaviour, as well as that of elephants, sun bears, dholes, Malayan tapirs, clouded leopards, black panthers, and golden and marbled cats. “Footage includes a graceful female tiger nicknamed the ‘Slender Tigress’, filmed hesitating at a muddy river before leaping across it, with another of a large male tiger looking directly at the camera unperturbed,” said Paolo, who has worked as a wildlife and conservation photographer for 20 years and produced stories for National Geographic Poland. He said the documentary was not only intended to show the tiger in distress, but also the beauty of the forest and the animals still living in it. Marta and Paolo are vice-­chairman and chairman, respectively, of the Clearwing Foun­dation for Biodiversity in Poland, which was set up in 2017 and counts a Malaysian among its co-founders. The 90-minute documentary is expected to be completed for airing next year. Follow us on our official WhatsApp channel for breaking news alerts and key updates! Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images Donald Trump ‘President of the Unites States’: White House’s AI accord includes spelling error Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI Ariana Baio Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.11 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The White House misspelled “United States” under the signature of Donald Trump on an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday. At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”. It is unclear how the misspelling occurred or whether it will appear in the Federal Register, the database that contains official presidential actions and other government documents. Trump and six tech executives signed the document voluntarily committing to safely developing AI to address widespread concerns, sparked by industry leaders who warned the technology is evolving too rapidly to control. Trump has largely brushed aside concerns about AI harming humans and called for companies to continue developing the technology so the US can become the global leader in AI. Even while signing the accord on safety, the US president praised the business executives for growth. Trump posted the document containing the misspelling on Truth Social , and the White House Communications Team emailed it out shortly after it was signed. The Bloomberg News correspondent David Gura appeared to be the first to notice the spelling error. The Guardian has asked the White House for comment The accord on artificial intelligence outlined four layers of “controls and audits” that companies will implement to ensure AI capabilities operate as intended. That includes “robust” internal controls and partnering with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”. Potential internal controls could include empowering a team to monitor and detect that AI is operating correctly and creating monitors to ensure AI technologies will not hack or access technical systems in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats. External monitors would also check to make sure the AI is operating as intended and companies could designate a committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from teams operating the controls of the AI. The accord is the first step in addressing concerns, raised by industry experts in mid-September. Americans have become increasingly skeptical of AI. A recent New York Times/Siena College poll found that 61% of voters opposed the construction of datacenters, while an SSRS/CNN poll found that 71% of Americans believed the government wasn’t doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI. While Tuesday’s document is only an accord, it left open the possibility of codifying the framework into formal regulations or laws – something Trump has repeatedly rejected. “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “And they understand that they have to self-police.” The six executives who signed the accord are Dario Amodei from Anthropic; Elon Musk from SpaceXAI; Greg Brockman from OpenAI; Jensen Huang from Nvidia; Mark Zuckerberg from Meta; and Sundar Pichai from Google.
